opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we looked at fairly closely in the s1 work. When you're thinking about test-time scaling, you want two things: control, meaning you can actually dictate how much compute the model spends, and scaling, meaning performance goes up as you give it more. Prompting with a token budget is the most obvious approach. You just tell the model, "think for up to 4,000 tokens," or whatever the number is.

In practice it doesn't work very well, at least not out of the box. Models are pretty bad at counting tokens. They don't have a good internal sense of how many tokens they've produced, so if you ask for a thousand you might get three hundred or three thousand. The control is weak. We tried a few variants. One was token-conditional, where you give the number directly. Another was step-conditional, where you say "use at most N reasoning steps." Steps are a bit easier for the model to track than raw tokens, so that does somewhat better. But then the model games it. If you limit the number of steps, it makes each step longer, so the total compute doesn't shrink the way you'd hope. There's also class-conditional prompting, where you say "think briefly" or "think for a long time." That gives you a rough knob, but it's coarse, and you can't really dial it in.

What ended up working much better for us was what we called budget forcing, which works at decoding time. If the model wants to stop before you think it should, you suppress the end-of-thinking delimiter and append something like "Wait," which nudges it to keep going and often to double-check its answer. If it's going over budget, you cut it off and force the end-of-thinking token so it has to answer. That gives you essentially perfect control, because you're enforcing the limit mechanically instead of hoping the model complies. And we saw a nice positive scaling slope, at least up to a point before it plateaus.

So my overall take is that prompting with a budget is appealing because it's simple and requires no changes to inference. But unless the model has been specifically trained to respect length instructions, it's unreliable. You can train for it, and I think that's a promising direction, things like adding length targets during RL. But if you want precise control today, intervening at decode time is much more dependable than just asking nicely in the prompt.

r001.rationale: The response says token-budget prompting “doesn't work very well” out of the box and explains that models may produce far fewer or more tokens than requested, so the control is weak.

r002.rationale: The response does not report results from supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces that respected prompted token limits or whether that led to reliable inference-time adherence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually something we looked at pretty closely in the s1 work, because the whole question there was: how do you control test-time compute? And the most obvious thing you can try is just telling the model. You put something in the prompt like "think for 500 tokens" or "use at most 2,000 tokens of reasoning" and hope it listens.

And the honest answer is that it kind of works, but not very well. What we found is that the model will shift its behavior a little bit in the direction you ask for — if you say a small budget, it'll reason somewhat less on average, and if you say a large budget, it'll reason somewhat more — but the correlation is pretty weak. It doesn't actually hit the number you give it. So you get this very noisy, very loose form of control. And more importantly, the scaling you get is not great. When we plotted accuracy against how much the model actually thought under different prompted budgets, the curve was pretty flat and in some cases it even went the wrong way. So you're not really getting the thing you want, which is a clean, monotonic relationship where more compute gives you better answers.

I think the reason is pretty intuitive. The model doesn't have a token counter. It's not really aware of how many tokens it has generated, so asking it to stop at a specific number is asking it to do something it has no internal signal for. It's a bit like asking a person to talk for exactly 90 seconds without a clock. You'll get roughly the right ballpark, but it's not precise, and the model often just ignores the instruction and does whatever it was going to do anyway.

That's actually what motivated budget forcing for us, which is much more of a hard intervention. Instead of asking nicely, you just truncate the thinking when it hits the limit and force the model to produce an answer, or if you want more thinking, you suppress the end-of-thinking token and append something like "Wait" so it keeps going. That gives you exact control. You know precisely how many tokens were used, and when we did that, we got the nice monotonic scaling we were looking for. More thinking, better accuracy, at least up to a point.

So my overall assessment is that prompting with a budget is a reasonable thing to try if you don't have access to the decoding loop — like if you're calling an API and you can only change the prompt — but it's a pretty blunt instrument. If you have any control over generation, intervening directly at the token level is much more reliable. And I'd add, this might get better over time. If labs train models explicitly to respect a budget in the prompt, with the budget as part of the training signal, then the model could learn an internal sense of length. I think we're seeing some of that now with models that offer reasoning effort settings. But for a model that wasn't trained for it, just putting a number in the prompt is more of a suggestion than a constraint.

r001.rationale: The response says prompted budgets shift reasoning length only somewhat, with weak correlation, and the model does not hit the specified token count reliably.

r002.rationale: It does not report that supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces respecting token limits failed at inference. It only speculates that explicitly training models to respect budgets could improve adherence.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful approach, but the question is how reliably the model follows that budget. You can tell it, “You have a thousand tokens to think,” but that doesn’t necessarily mean it will stop after a thousand tokens, or use those tokens well. It has to understand how to allocate its reasoning within that constraint.

I’d distinguish that from actually enforcing a budget at inference time, where you control when the model has to move from thinking to answering. Prompting gives the model more flexibility, which could be valuable, but I’d want to measure both budget adherence and answer quality. Does it actually give you a better trade-off between compute and accuracy, or does it just make the reasoning shorter?

r001.rationale: It says telling the model to think for a set number of tokens does not necessarily make it stop at that limit.

r002.rationale: It does not mention supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces or its effect on inference-time adherence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful approach, but there’s a distinction between asking the model to use a certain number of tokens and actually enforcing that budget. You can prompt it to think for, say, a thousand tokens, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it will follow that instruction precisely. And counting tokens is itself a difficult task for the model.

So I’d assess it along two dimensions: how reliably does it stay within the budget, and what happens to accuracy as you change that budget? Ultimately, you want more control over the tradeoff between compute and performance. If the model spends longer reasoning but doesn’t get better answers, then following the budget alone isn’t particularly useful.

r001.rationale: It says prompting for a specific token count does not mean the model will follow the instruction precisely.
